conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility (who must turn extractor on / standing rule)
window vs. laundry (risk of wetting laundry if window opened)
dialogue_quality_notes: Conversation is concise and goal-directed: repeated short time-checks (5 min → 3 min → 1 min → 30s) move the interaction toward release of the stove.
Agent B persistently presses for a standing rule; Agent A consistently prioritizes immediate constraints (laundry blocking window) and refuses a blanket rule.
Practical actions are recorded in public updates (extractor turned on, stove freed), which grounds the negotiation.
No third-party enforcement or formal rule-setting occurs; resolution is bilateral and pragmatic.
evaluation.final_reason: Agents reached a practical, conditional agreement: Agent A pledged to run the extractor for 10 minutes now and to turn it on for noticeably smelly cooking or when asked; Agent B accepted this expectation. The broader policy demand for an automatic always-on rule making the cook solely responsible remains explicitly refused by Agent A, so the dispute is only partially resolved (practical behavior agreed; formal standing rule unresolved).
position_change_notes: Agent A shifted from resisting immediate demands to making a specific conditional commitment: agreed to run the extractor now and to use it for smelly cooking or when asked, but explicitly refused an automatic always-on duty.
Agent B shifted from insisting on a standing rule to accepting a practical expectation and monitoring: 'If it doesn't happen, we'll address it again.'
Agent C's position (not consenting to moving the drying rack) remained unaltered and continued to constrain the window option.
No one else changed position regarding stove access after Agent A freed it; stove-access issue was directly resolved.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demands a standing rule: 'Can you agree to always turn it on when you cook?' while Agent A only agrees to turn the extractor on now ('I'll turn the extractor on. I'm almost done—give me five minutes') — the dispute over who should be responsible for ventilation and whether a standing rule will be imposed remains active.

Agent B reiterates the rule/duty demand and extends it ('Will you agree to always turn the extractor on before you cook and leave it on until the smell's gone?'), while Agent A requests more time to finish; conflict about a standing responsibility and immediate management of ventilation remains unresolved.

Agent B continues to press for an agreement about extractor usage ('After you're done, keep the extractor on for 10 minutes so the smell clears. Do you agree?') and Agent A delays finishing — substantive disagreement about commitments and responsibility persists.

Agent B again asks for confirmation of a standing behavior ('Please keep the extractor on for 10 minutes after you're done so the smell clears, and confirm you'll always switch it on when you cook'), while Agent A continues to delay finishing; the core disagreement about an always-on/ cook-responsibility rule is still live.

Agent A frees the stove and agrees to run the extractor for 10 minutes ('Done — stove's free. I'll leave the extractor on for 10 minutes') but explicitly refuses the standing rule ('I won't agree to a standing 'always-on' rule that makes the cook responsible every time'), so the immediate practical conflict (stove access, extractor now running) is settled while the policy-level disagreement about a permanent rule remains.

Agent A restates a conditional commitment ('I'll turn it on when I'm cooking something that makes noticeable smells or when you ask. I won't agree to an automatic always-on rule') and Agent B accepts this expectation ('Okay — that's acceptable... If it doesn't happen, we'll address it again'), leaving only a minor unresolved matter about creating a formal automatic rule.

substantive_insights: Tension separates immediate practical mitigation (turn extractor on now; run 10 minutes) from governance (who bears ongoing responsibility).
Physical constraint (laundry blocking the window and risk of wetting clothes) reduces available ventilation options, making conditional agreements more realistic than an unconditional rule.
Resolving immediate operational needs (freeing the stove, running the extractor) made further escalation unnecessary and enabled a compromise about future behaviour.

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 6 because the final status is partially_resolved.
